A final norm at the end of each stack
Each stack now ends with its own

rows at a predictable scale again.
This is what the change costs, and it is easy to miss. With post-norm the last thing every layer did was normalise, so
the encoder’s output was always at a predictable scale. With pre-norm it is not: the last layer returns x, which is the
embeddings plus every correction ever added, never rescaled. So both stacks now end with a
each. The panel shows what the last encoder layer returns,

Post-norm is not wrong — it is harder to train
used is the one in the original paper, and it produced every result that made Transformers famous. The case for moving the norm is about trainability at depth, not correctness.
what the residual path passes through
the pre-norm shortcut is what keeps deep stacks trainable
attention sees inputs at a predictable scale either way
needs careful warmup and may still diverge
the reason every modern model is pre-norm
is two statistics and a division

sounds technical, but it is only three steps on one row of numbers: find their mean, subtract it, and divide by their standard deviation. Both statistics come from the row itself, so nothing about the other sentence, the other words or the batch size can affect the result.
